entities.summary:
Grosolanus (also known as Grossolanus), born Peter, served as the Archbishop of Milan from 1102 until his deposition in 1112, a tumultuous decade marked by intense clashes between imperial and papal authority during the Investiture Controversy. His tenure represented a critical phase in the long struggle for control over episcopal appointments in Lombardy, positioning Milan at the heart of wider European ecclesiastical politics. Succeeding Anselm IV, who had appointed him vicar before departing on the ill-fated Crusade of 1101, Grosolanus's episcopacy was inextricably linked to the volatile relationship between Emperor Henry V and Pope Paschal II, defining the local church's allegiance and autonomy.

His archiepiscopal election in 1102 was contentious, taking place amidst a power vacuum following Anselm IV's death and a period of significant political instability within the city. Initially supported by Emperor Henry V, Grosolanus found his authority challenged by the Milanese populace and local clergy who favored papal nominees, reflecting the deep divisions within the city's ecclesiastical landscape. He was consecrated by Pope Paschal II in Rome, an act that temporarily legitimized his position but did not resolve the underlying tensions. Throughout his ten years, Grosolanus actively participated in synods and diplomatic efforts aimed at resolving the Investiture Controversy, notably attending the Synod of Guastalla in 1106 and engaging with both imperial and papal legates.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Grosolanus's tumultuous decade as Archbishop of Milan highlights the intense regional impact of the Investiture Controversy, directly influencing the power dynamics between the papacy, the Holy Roman Emperor, and burgeoning urban communes. His deposition by popular and clerical will demonstrates a critical shift towards local ecclesiastical and civic autonomy.
